---
title: "Normal–normal posterior shrinkage"
subtitle: "1.5 · a teaching prior, after Kline, Rose and Walters (2024) and Walters' teaching slides"
description: "Precision-weighted posterior means and changes in pairwise order under a common normal prior."
---

Under a normal likelihood and a common normal prior, the posterior mean averages the estimate and the prior mean, weighting each by its precision. Those precisions are the inverse squared standard error and the inverse prior variance. The resulting mean minimizes posterior expected squared error. The figure traces the change from each estimate $\hat\theta_i$ in vermilion to its posterior mean in navy. Estimates with larger standard errors move farther toward the prior mean. When the standard errors differ, the order can change. A common standard error preserves the order.

## Numerical illustrations {#what-to-try}

- **Prior SD .15.** Small units move .64 of the way to 0, medium units .31 and large units .10. The units move toward 0 by different amounts, reversing the estimated order for 37 of the 435 pairs in this draw.
- **Prior SD .05.** A narrower prior increases shrinkage: small units move .94, large units .50, and in this draw 71 of the
  435 pairs change order.
- **Every SE .10.** A common SE gives a common retained share, .69, for every unit: no lines cross, and 0 of the 435 pairs change
  order.
- **Against the true values.** In this draw the average squared distance to the true values (crosses) falls from
  .0163 to .0096 and the spread from .162 to .098, below the truth's .149; yet 14 of 30 units end farther (ringed).
- **Too narrow a prior.** A prior too narrow for these true values can even raise the average: at prior SD .02,
  .0197 against the estimates' .0163 in this draw, and .0191 against .0175 over many draws.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), KRW, estimate their prior from all the firms (section III, slide 49); it is not
normal, depends on each firm's SE (section V.B) and, for race, puts all its weight on positive gaps. So State Farm's
race estimate of −.544 (SE .444) has a posterior mean of .155 (90% interval .014 to .342, from a smoothed version of
KRW's posteriors). In their data, ranks from linear (James–Stein-type) shrinkage "perform substantially worse than
naively ranking the point estimates" (section V.E). The postrank theory book (ch. 20, "Empirical Bayes specification")
sets out their prior; the normal prior here is a teaching simplification. Data: Kline, Rose and Walters (2024),
doi:10.1257/aer.20230700, and deposit doi:10.3886/E198284V1; CC-BY-NC as stated by the deposit (no version),
noncommercial use only; as adapted in postrank 1.1.0 (pr_case_krw), changes noted; no endorsement by the authors is
implied. The data describe KRW's correspondence experiment, not any firm's current conduct.
:::
